Scripture uses it broadly in passages connected with creation, commands, judgment, death, and what God gives or does for people. It occurs 552 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise reference may be an individual man or humanity more generally, depending on the sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “bottle,” naming a concrete physical object. It functions as a noun for something mentioned in ordinary actions and speech, rather than expressing an abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in 1 Kings and twice in Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains a bottle or similar container.

This Hebrew word means “ends,” referring to the terminal parts or outer limits of something. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Exodus. In each occurrence, it functions as a concrete noun connected with an object being made or described, so it identifies the object’s ending portions rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the item being discussed.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose ordinary English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Jeremiah 48:37, but the verse text and an approved meaning phrase are not available here. Its precise sense therefore requires the surrounding verse and related language rather than a confident standalone definition. The word’s identity is preserved as a Hebrew term and should not be given an invented translation or expanded beyond what Scripture’s context establishes.

This Hebrew noun refers to grasshoppers or locusts—swarming insects known for appearing in large numbers. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, in two verses, and English translations render it with these two closely related terms. Its meaning is therefore concrete and consistent: it identifies the insects themselves rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The precise force of the word in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of these creatures.

This Hebrew word means “rebuke.” It refers to a firm expression of correction or displeasure, directed against someone or something. As a noun, it names the rebuke itself rather than the action of speaking it. The word occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in passages describing the force of God’s command or correction. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Hosea 1:3, and is rendered “Diblaim.” Its recorded use is connected with a family or genealogy setting and with birth or begetting, so its main function is as a name within that lineage. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific role there.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “drams,” a monetary unit or amount given in the accounts of the returning exiles. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, and each occurrence functions as the object of giving. The word therefore names something that people contributed or presented, rather than describing a person, action, or quality. Its use is closely connected with recorded gifts for the work of the restored community.

This Hebrew word expresses “Woe,” a cry of grief, distress, or warning. It is an interjection used to draw attention to serious trouble or impending judgment, rather than a word naming a person or object. In the Old Testament, it appears 51 times, especially in Isaiah and Jeremiah, where it commonly introduces a solemn announcement against wrongdoing or disastrous conditions. It can also express deep sorrow in a lament. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

“Behold” is an attention-directing word that calls the reader or hearer to notice what follows. It can introduce a person, circumstance, statement, or significant development, giving the words that follow special focus. This Hebrew word occurs 318 times in the Old Testament, so it serves as a recurring way to point out something important rather than naming an object or action itself. Its precise emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Hebrew word means “loathsome.” It functions as a descriptive word for something regarded with strong disgust or rejection. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Numbers 11:20. Because the available material provides no surrounding verse text, its broader force in that particular sentence cannot be explained here; the secure lexical sense is the description of something viewed with strong disgust or rejection.

Azaniah is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nehemiah 10:9. Since the available rendering is simply “Azaniah,” the word’s primary function is identification: it names a person mentioned in that passage. Its specific significance beyond identifying that individual must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

Halhul is a proper name for a place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it refers to a location listed among the cities of the hill country of Judah. The word occurs once, in Joshua 15:58, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Halhul.” Because it functions as a place name rather than a descriptive term, its ordinary meaning is the identification of that location, not a quality or action. The surrounding verse gives the specific setting for its listing.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Hamor.” It functions as a proper name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs 13 times, chiefly in Genesis, and appears in passages where Hamor is named or spoken about. Its ordinary meaning is therefore a person’s name, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular role or significance associated with him.

The word means “Harodite,” functioning as a designation that identifies a person. It is not presented here as a general action, quality, or object, but as a name-like identifier attached to an individual. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs twice, both within 2 Samuel 23:25. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense supplied is simply “Harodite.”

This Hebrew word refers to a radiant substance described as “amber” or “metal.” It names the bright, shining material seen in Ezekiel’s visions, rather than an action or quality. The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ezekiel. Its repeated use in those visions presents a distinctive gleaming substance associated with what Ezekiel saw. The surrounding verse determines how the image functions in each passage.

e.t: This word means “river,” referring to a substantial flowing waterway. It is used as a noun for a river as a physical feature, including the river associated with Egypt in passages from Genesis and Exodus. The word occurs 65 times in the Hebrew Bible, so it commonly identifies a significant river within a scene, command, journey, or prophetic image. Its normal meaning remains the same when the river is connected with life, danger, judgment, or the movement of people and water.

This Hebrew verb expresses knowing something or making something known. It can describe information being recognized, understood, revealed, or communicated, depending on how it functions in the sentence. Its approved meaning range includes “known” and “make,” showing that the word may point either to knowledge itself or to the act of bringing knowledge to others. It occurs 47 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Ezra and Daniel, where it commonly serves in statements about information being known, declared, or made clear.

This Hebrew word refers to “mules,” describing the animal named in Genesis 36:24. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, so its ordinary meaning is narrow rather than a broad recurring concept. In that passage, it functions as the name of a concrete animal, not as an abstract quality or action. The surrounding verse supplies the specific scene in which the animal is mentioned; the word itself identifies what is being referred to.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “shovels,” tools used among the furnishings and equipment connected with Israel’s tabernacle and temple worship. It appears nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including descriptions of items made for the altar and other sacred service. The word can also appear in accounts of temple vessels being carried away, showing that these were recognizable implements rather than abstract terms. Its normal meaning is therefore a practical tool used in handling material during worship or related temple service.

e.t: Ithream is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, in 2 Samuel 3:5 and 1 Chronicles 3:3. Its recorded use belongs to genealogical material, where it identifies one of David’s sons. Because it functions as a name, its ordinary meaning for readers is the person designated by “Ithream,” not a general word or character trait.

Cushan is a proper name, rendered “Cushan,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Habakkuk 3:7. It identifies a named referent in that passage, while the surrounding verse and passage determine exactly whom or what the name denotes. The word itself contributes the name Cushan, not a separate quality, action, or description.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “shame,” referring to disgrace or humiliation. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Jeremiah 23:40, so its normal biblical use is represented by that single occurrence. The word functions as a noun naming an unwanted condition or outcome, rather than an action. Its associated scriptural pattern places this shame among things that can be given or brought upon someone, while the precise force in Jeremiah depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible, at 1 Samuel 21:8, but no gloss, short definition, or approved fallback meaning is available here. Its identity is preserved as a distinct Hebrew word, yet the verse text and surrounding context are not provided, so a more specific English meaning would be guesswork.

This Hebrew verb means “dig.” It describes making an opening or hollow in the ground, and it can also express the action of digging into something. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized term. Its use as a predicate presents digging as something a person or group does, whether preparing a place, opening the ground, or figuratively dealing harmfully with another person. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to later growth—something that comes after an earlier stage of growth. In the Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Amos 7:1, with English renderings of “growth” and “latter.” Its basic sense therefore points to growth associated with what is later. The precise force of the word in Amos 7:1 depends on the surrounding verse context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “expectation.” It names what is anticipated or looked toward. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, appearing twice in Isaiah and once in Zechariah. Its recorded uses place this expectation within statements about people and their outlook, so it describes an object of attention or speech rather than an action. The precise force in any verse comes from its surrounding passage.

“Ruin” is the clearest supported meaning of this Hebrew Old Testament word. It refers to ruin as a thing or condition named in a sentence, rather than supplying an action or description. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Proverbs 26:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical idea remains straightforward: it names ruin.

This Hebrew word means “Lament,” expressing an act of mourning or sorrow. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joel 1:8. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that verse must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a call or expression to lament.

Mahazioth is a Hebrew name preserved as a proper name rather than rendered as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles 25, and the English form remains “Mahazioth.” No broader translated meaning is established here, so the safest understanding is the person’s name itself, not a claim about a wider concept. Its precise significance in either verse requires the surrounding passage.

“Cords” refers to lines or lengths used to tie, secure, or support something. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this noun describes a practical object, including cords connected with the tabernacle and its furnishings. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, consistently pointing to a concrete object rather than an abstract idea. Its exact function—such as securing, supporting, or marking an area—depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “highway,” referring to a traveled way or road. It functions as a noun naming a route people use to go from one place to another. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, including passages where people travel along or observe such a way. Its normal sense remains a physical path of travel, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which it appears.

Makheloth is a Hebrew proper name identifying a location, rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Makheloth” and appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33:25–26. As a place-name, its meaning is primarily its identity as a named location; the word itself is not translated into a broader descriptive idea. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Merodach is a personal name, rendered “Merodach” in English. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Isaiah 39:1. The available wording identifies the person by name but does not provide a broader lexical definition, such as an ordinary action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, while the word itself functions as a proper name rather than a general descriptive term.

The word means “morning,” referring to the beginning portion of the day. It is a noun used to name that time rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 6:19. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear and direct: morning. This is a simple time word, identifying the day’s morning period rather than expressing an event, feeling, or command.

“Fleeth” is an action word describing a person moving away from a threatening situation or pursuing force. It focuses on the person's response, rather than naming the danger itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, this word occurs once, at Jeremiah 48:44. Since the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is an act of rapid departure from danger.

This Hebrew verb means "yell": to cry out loudly rather than speak quietly. It describes an audible outburst or shout, and its basic force is the act of raising one's voice. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 51:38. Since no verse text is provided here, the surrounding situation cannot be described without adding meaning beyond the word itself. Its precise force in that occurrence therefore depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes piercing, thrusting, or picking into something. Its central idea is making a penetrating action, whether by driving something into a person or object, piercing with force, or picking at something. The approved rendering “pierced” captures this basic sense. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with related uses appearing in passages from Numbers, Judges, 1 Samuel, Job, Proverbs, and Isaiah. The exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being pierced or struck and the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to “drink” or being “drunken.” It describes alcohol or the condition associated with excessive drinking, rather than naming a person or place. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, with its uses rendered as “drink” and “drunken.” Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea consistently concerns intoxicating drink and drunkenness.

Its occurrences are found in Ezra and Nehemiah. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the condition itself or on release from it.

e.t: This word is a personal name, rendered “Uzza.” It identifies people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 14 times in 14 verses, including passages that refer to Uzza in the books of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name appears in genealogical material as well as historical accounts, so its exact reference depends on the surrounding passage. Its ordinary function is simply to name a person.

This Hebrew word expresses something being concealed or kept out of sight. It is commonly rendered “hide,” and it can also function with the sense “from,” marking what is hidden from someone or removed from notice. Across its 28 Old Testament occurrences, it describes matters that are not openly seen, recognized, or known. Its precise force depends on the sentence, but the central idea is concealment or absence from a person’s awareness.

Its uses include descriptions connected with human ability and with what God formed, so the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being described. The word’s central idea remains a direct description of strength rather than an action or command.

Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a binding restraint.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “wonders”—extraordinary acts or works that inspire awe. In the Old Testament, it commonly describes works associated with God, including acts remembered in worship and declarations of what God has done. It occurs 13 times in 13 Old Testament verses, especially in the Psalms. The word can also describe wondrous matters connected with birth, death, and the unfolding of what is yet to come. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word means “youth.” It functions as a noun, referring to youth as a person or group. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 30:12, so its normal meaning is established from this single occurrence and its English rendering. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains “youth.”

This Hebrew word expresses being “destroyed,” describing the removal or defeat of something. It functions as a verb in the Old Testament and appears three times, each in a different verse. Its use therefore centers on an action that brings something to an end rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The repeated rendering “destroyed” provides the clearest supported sense for understanding this word across its limited occurrences.

This Hebrew word refers to a young bird, such as a chick or fledgling. It is a noun used for birds that are still young, rather than for a bird in general. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three verses: Deuteronomy 22:6, Job 39:30, and Psalm 84:3. Its use in these passages keeps the focus on young birds as distinct from the mother bird, helping readers recognize that the word names the young creature itself. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes something “dry,” referring to a condition marked by the absence of moisture. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Isaiah, so its normal sense is narrowly represented in this corpus. As a descriptive term, it identifies the quality of what is being spoken about rather than naming a person, place, or action. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing described there.

The Hebrew word צְנָן is rendered “Zenan,” so it functions as a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew corpus, at Joshua 15:37, and the English renderings preserve the same name. Because no explicit lexical definition or verse text is available here, the safest meaning is the identified name itself: Zenan. Its precise significance belongs to the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a grave—the place where a dead person is buried. It can also describe graves collectively. Scripture uses it for burial places connected with family members, kings, prophets, and others who have died. The word occurs 67 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent meaning centered on the physical place of burial. Its precise significance in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains a grave or graves.

“Wither” means to dry up, lose freshness, or become weakened, and this Hebrew word functions as a verb describing that kind of decline. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Isaiah. Its English rendering is “wither” in both occurrences, giving a consistent basic sense. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its imagery, but the central picture is something becoming dry, lifeless, or diminished.

This Hebrew noun means “war.” It names war as a thing or condition, rather than describing an action, person, or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 7:21, and its recorded English rendering is consistently “war.” The precise force of the word in that verse depends on Daniel 7:21 and its surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning is simply war.

This Hebrew verb describes people acting together in a harmful or secret plan—“conspired.” It functions as an action word, showing what people do rather than naming a person or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 44 times and is especially associated with people joining against others or working together toward an opposing purpose. Its use at 1 Samuel 22:8 and 1 Kings 16:16 reflects this recurring sense of coordinated opposition.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “many,” describing people or things as numerous or increasing in number. It functions in sentences to indicate that a quantity has become large or that something is multiplying. In the Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, including descriptions of people becoming numerous and enemies being numerous. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense concerns quantity becoming great.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes something as “vain,” marking it as unable to provide the result, substance, or value expected from it. It functions as a description of things, actions, plans, or pursuits that do not accomplish their intended purpose. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, where it consistently presents what is empty of dependable outcome rather than fruitful or effective.

This Hebrew word means “merchants,” identifying people engaged in buying, selling, or transporting goods. It commonly refers to traders in commercial settings, including those associated with valuable products and international exchange. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Ezekiel and several in Nehemiah. Its precise role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew verb expresses the action “brandished”—to wave or display something forcefully. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nahum 2:3, so its normal scriptural use is attested in only that single passage. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding verse text and context.

This Hebrew verb means “magnify”: it names an action of magnifying. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Job. As a verb, it expresses what someone does toward a person or matter. Its two occurrences provide a focused picture of this action rather than a complete range of uses, while the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to an “accusation” made against someone. It occurs once in the Old Testament, in Ezra 4:6, and functions as something directed against a person or group. Its relationship with the verb for writing indicates that the accusation was presented in written form. The word therefore describes a formal statement of wrongdoing or opposition, rather than a general feeling of disapproval. Its precise force in Ezra 4:6 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Solomon,” referring to the son of David and a prominent king of Israel. It functions as a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears 293 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Kings and Chronicles, where it identifies Solomon in genealogies, royal succession, speech, giving, and other recorded events. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Shepho is a personal name, also rendered Shephi. It identifies a person in the Old Testament rather than expressing a general quality, action, or theological idea. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible, once in Genesis 36:23 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:40. Because the available passages do not provide a meaning or definition for the name itself, its ordinary sense is limited to its use as a personal designation. The two English renderings reflect the same Hebrew name in these genealogical references.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “judgments.” It names judgments as the object of statements and actions: Scripture presents them as something spoken, made, or given. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 16 times, including passages in Exodus, Proverbs, 2 Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its repeated use with speech and action shows that the word can refer to judgments that are declared or carried out.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cuttings,” referring to something produced by cutting. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Leviticus. In its recorded uses, it functions as the object of an action involving cutting, so the word identifies what is cut or the resulting cuttings rather than naming the action itself. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains cuttings.

e.t: The word means “integrity,” expressing a quality or condition rather than an action. It is used in the Hebrew Old Testament as a noun-like expression, describing the state associated with a person, thing, or circumstance. It occurs 24 times across 24 verses, so its basic idea appears in varied settings. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The Hebrew word refers to “Tammuz,” a proper name rather than a general description or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 8:14. Because it functions as a name, its basic role is to identify the person or figure designated by that name; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular significance there. The English rendering preserves the name as Tammuz.

This Hebrew word is a place-name, rendered with the names “Beer” and “Lahai,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular location in Genesis. The name occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within three verses: Genesis 16:14, 24:62, and 25:11. Its exact significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: Agag is a personal name, rendered “Agag,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs eight times, appearing once in Numbers and seven times in 1 Samuel. Its occurrences function as a named individual within statements and relationships, so its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This word describes “terror” or “trouble”: a condition of frightening distress that overwhelms or afflicts people. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, and its uses point to severe circumstances rather than a casual worry. It can name the frightening condition itself, whether people endure it or it comes upon them. The central idea is a deeply disturbing experience marked by fear and hardship. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.
